paragraphs: Data may occupy a low-dimensional manifold even when each observation has many coordinates. This paper studies whether a small collection of random linear measurements retains enough information to discover that hidden structure. The manifold is unknown, so dimensionality reduction must work without first constructing a detailed geometric model.

The authors show that intrinsic dimension can be estimated accurately from random projections of sampled points. They also prove that the underlying manifold’s structure can be estimated using only those projected measurements. In both results, the required projection count grows linearly with intrinsic dimension and logarithmically with ambient dimension.

The contribution connects simple linear compression with nonlinear geometric discovery. It suggests that learning the relevant dimension and structure need not begin with full high-dimensional observations when the data satisfy the manifold model. The supplied abstract ends mid-sentence, so the summary relies on its complete statements rather than inferring additional guarantees beyond them.
neurips-2007-random-projections-for-mani.tldr: A small set of random projections can preserve enough information to estimate intrinsic dimension and manifold structure.

paragraphs: Continuous-action reinforcement learning must find a good action as well as estimate how valuable actions are. Unlike a small discrete action set, the alternatives cannot simply all be checked. This paper uses sequential Monte Carlo to represent and update an actor’s policy within an actor–critic method.

The critic supplies learned values that guide importance sampling. A resampling step then changes the actor’s action distribution, concentrating its representation on promising choices. This gives a particle-based route to policy improvement that naturally handles a continuous space instead of requiring an explicit enumeration of all actions.

The approach is compared empirically with other learning methods, including a river-crossing task in which a boat must be steered. The contribution combines value learning with an adaptive sampling mechanism for action selection. It addresses the optimization bottleneck specific to continuous controls: learning a useful value surface is not enough unless the agent can efficiently choose actions from it.
neurips-2007-reinforcement-learning-in-c.tldr: A sequential-Monte-Carlo actor uses critic values for importance sampling and resampling to learn policies over continuous actions.

paragraphs: Structured prediction often needs approximate inference because finding the best labeling is computationally hard. A good approximation to the score, however, may not be a good component of a learning algorithm. This paper shows why inference quality and learning compatibility must be analyzed together.

Approximate inference can make some predictions unreachable even when the underlying model could represent them. It can also react to parameter changes in ways that mislead standard update rules. Consequently, learning may fail despite a rigorous approximation guarantee for the inference procedure considered on its own.

The authors also give positive learning bounds for linear-programming-relaxed inference in structured perceptron and empirical-risk-minimization settings. These results identify compatible combinations rather than condemning approximate inference generally. The contribution is a precise warning and a constructive alternative: a useful guarantee must describe the interaction between the learner and its inference routine, not only the quality of isolated decoding.
neurips-2007-structured-learning-with-ap.tldr: Approximate inference can break structured learning despite score guarantees; compatible LP-relaxed combinations receive positive learning bounds.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene involves interdependent tasks such as identifying objects, labeling regions, and estimating 3D structure. Strong standalone classifiers do not automatically benefit from one another. Cascaded Classification Models provide a way to connect such systems while allowing each to retain its own specialized implementation.

Repeated instances of the classifiers are linked through their input and output variables in a cascade. Later stages use earlier predictions to improve their own tasks and supply better information to others. A limited black-box interface avoids the need to redesign the internal workings of sophisticated component models.

On a large natural-image collection, the framework combines scene categorization, object detection, multiclass segmentation, and 3D reconstruction effectively. The contribution is a learned coordination scheme for holistic understanding. It shows how relationships among tasks can be used operationally, making joint performance improve through exchanged predictions rather than requiring one monolithic model for every aspect of the scene.
neurips-2008-cascaded-classification-mod.tldr: Cascaded Classification Models let specialized scene-understanding systems exchange predictions and improve together through a black-box interface.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process posterior functions can be strongly correlated, making direct sampling inefficient. This paper introduces a lower-dimensional set of auxiliary function values to guide the sampling process. Those control variables provide a manageable handle on changes to the full function.

At each Markov-chain step, the method proposes new control-variable values and draws the remaining function from the conditional Gaussian-process prior. Their input locations are optimized continuously through an objective function. The procedure therefore adapts where its compact representation is anchored rather than fixing those locations arbitrarily.

Demonstrations include regression, classification, and parameter estimation for a differential-equation model of gene regulation. The contribution is an inference strategy that combines compact proposals with the full process’s conditional structure. It addresses correlation in function-space sampling while retaining a probabilistic representation of uncertainty, rather than replacing posterior inference with a single fitted function.
neurips-2008-efficient-sampling-for-gaus.tldr: Adaptive control variables make Gaussian-process posterior sampling more efficient by proposing compact function summaries and sampling conditional completions.

paragraphs: Online algorithms can learn efficiently from sequential examples, but their evolving predictors must be converted into a final model for ordinary batch use. Existing conversion methods can work unevenly across online learners. Cutoff averaging is designed to adapt that conversion to the behavior of the underlying conservative algorithm.

The technique combines information from the online learning process while explicitly accounting for the algorithm being converted. It preserves the computational efficiency of the original learner, making the conversion suitable for large datasets. This addresses model aggregation without replacing the efficient training procedure that produced the predictors.

The authors provide statistical analysis and experimental support. The contribution is a general online-to-batch construction for conservative learners, with adaptability as its distinguishing feature. It treats the final-predictor choice as an important part of learning: a fast sequence of updates becomes a useful batch method only when that sequence is summarized in a statistically appropriate way.
neurips-2008-from-online-to-batch-learni.tldr: Cutoff averaging adapts online-to-batch conversion to conservative learners while preserving their computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Unlabeled examples sometimes greatly reduce the number of labels needed for classification and sometimes provide little benefit. This uneven empirical picture has been difficult to reconcile with broad theoretical claims. The paper develops a framework for specifying when semi-supervised learning can genuinely improve performance.

The analysis gives finite-sample error bounds that quantify possible gains from unlabeled data. It identifies large classes of problems where semi-supervised methods outperform supervised learning, including settings with better error-convergence rates. The framework thus examines conditions and magnitudes of improvement rather than assuming unlabeled data are uniformly useful.

The contribution connects practical success to a more discriminating theory of learnability. Its central implication is that the usefulness of the input distribution depends on the structure of the learning problem. More unlabeled observations are valuable when that structure connects them to the prediction target, and a meaningful guarantee must make those favorable conditions explicit.
neurips-2008-unlabeled-data-now-it-helps.tldr: A finite-sample framework identifies broad problem classes where unlabeled data improve label efficiency and sometimes convergence rates.

paragraphs: Graph matching often optimizes a continuous relaxation and only afterward rounds it to a discrete assignment. That final step can discard much of the apparent improvement in the relaxed objective. This paper makes discrete solution construction a central part of an algorithm for matching and MAP inference.

The integer projected fixed-point method optimizes a quadratic score incorporating individual-feature similarity and pairwise geometry. It has ascent and convergence properties and can run independently or refine the output of another matching algorithm. In MAP inference, it forms a parallel extension of Iterated Conditional Modes.

Experiments outperform existing graph-matching methods and improve them further when used as a refinement stage. MAP tests also surpass ICM and Max-Product Belief Propagation. The contribution emphasizes that progress must survive the discrete constraints of the original task; a high-quality relaxed solution is only useful if the algorithm can turn it into a good feasible prediction.
neurips-2009-an-integer-projected-fixed-.tldr: Integer projected fixed-point optimization improves graph matching and MAP inference by treating discrete assignments as part of optimization.

paragraphs: People remember the order of historical events or physical quantities imperfectly, but their errors need not be identical. This paper asks whether combining several remembered rankings can recover a more accurate ordering. The data come from general-knowledge tasks requiring participants to reconstruct order from memory.

Two Bayesian aggregation models use Thurstonian and Mallows formulations. Each allows a person’s answer to arise either from a noisy version of the hidden true ordering or from guessing. Markov-chain Monte Carlo jointly infers the underlying order and the strategies that best explain individual responses.

The aggregated rankings are closer to the truth than the best individual ranking, demonstrating a wisdom-of-crowds effect for order information. The contribution shows how an explicit model of memory noise and guessing can extract shared structure from imperfect recollections. Combining answers is valuable here because the model distinguishes informative variation from responses that carry little ordering evidence.
neurips-2009-the-wisdom-of-crowds-in-the.tldr: Bayesian models aggregate noisy remembered rankings into orderings more accurate than those of the best individual participant.

paragraphs: High treewidth usually makes probabilistic inference difficult, limiting the structures learned by tractable Markov-network methods. This paper exploits context-specific independence and determinism to learn a broader class of models. A graph can appear complex globally while decomposing into simpler pieces under particular conditions.

The algorithm searches for features that partition the state space into regions where remaining variables become independent subsets. It then recurses within those regions and subsets. Under bounded feature length and bounded dependency strength, the authors give probabilistic performance guarantees, even when treewidth is much larger than the feature length.

A faster greedy version sacrifices those guarantees for practicality. Across several domains, the approach compares favorably with thin junction trees and other structure learners. The contribution shows how tractability can come from conditional structure rather than graph sparsity alone, preserving desirable properties such as polynomial inference and closed-form weight learning in a richer model class.
neurips-2010-learning-efficient-markov-n.tldr: Context-specific decomposition enables learning high-treewidth Markov networks that still support tractable inference and efficient parameter estimation.

paragraphs: Recovering a graphical model from data means deciding which variable pairs have direct conditional relationships. In high dimensions, that decision must use limited samples and manageable computation. This paper proposes a local conditional-mutual-information test for selecting Ising and Gaussian graph structures.

The threshold-based algorithm relies only on low-order statistics and tests whether two nodes should be neighbors. Under stated structural assumptions, it consistently recovers the graph when the sample count scales as Ω(Jmin⁻⁴ log p), where p is the number of variables and Jmin is the smallest edge strength.

The authors also derive nonasymptotic necessary conditions for graphical-model selection. The contribution combines a simple estimator with both sufficient and limiting sample requirements. Its dependence on minimum edge strength is informative: weak interactions are harder to distinguish reliably, so logarithmic growth in the number of variables does not by itself determine the difficulty of recovery.
neurips-2011-high-dimensional-graphical-.tldr: Low-order conditional-mutual-information tests recover specified Ising and Gaussian graph families with explicit sample-complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Seeing one feature of an unfamiliar animal often prompts expectations about other features, such as where it lives or how it moves. This paper asks what knowledge supports those inferences. It compares abstract relationships among features with memories of specific previously encountered animals.

A graphical model formalizes dependency-based reasoning, while a family of exemplar models formalizes comparison with known creatures. Participants reason about chimeras whose feature pairs have not previously appeared together. These unusual combinations help distinguish general relational knowledge from simple similarity to familiar examples.

The results favor explicit representations of relationships among features. The contribution is an experimental test of how people generalize beyond stored instances when a new combination breaks familiar patterns. It suggests that category knowledge can include reusable dependencies, allowing inference about a novel creature without requiring a close match to an animal already known.
neurips-2011-inductive-reasoning-about-c.tldr: Reasoning about novel chimeric animals supports feature-dependency representations over purely exemplar-based accounts of human induction.

paragraphs: Interaction networks are often inferred from noisy pairwise scores, but the properties of the entities themselves can supply additional information. This paper combines those sources to estimate relationships and discover groups jointly. Its model extends the Indian Buffet Process, a Bayesian nonparametric latent-feature framework.

The extension integrates uncertain interaction evidence with individual entity attributes. This allows network inference and node clustering to inform one another instead of being performed as disconnected steps. The application examines how microRNAs regulate messenger RNAs, where recovering the right interactions is biologically meaningful.

Synthetic and real-data analyses improve on prior methods, recover interactions and clusters, and yield accurate biological predictions. The contribution is a flexible model for sharing information between network structure and node properties. The latent representation provides a way to pool weak evidence across related entities rather than treating every candidate interaction as an independent classification problem.
neurips-2011-inferring-interaction-netwo.tldr: An Indian Buffet Process extension combines node attributes and noisy interaction scores to infer networks and latent groups, including microRNA targets.

paragraphs: A document’s words reflect more than its topic: they can also reveal discipline, perspective, sentiment, or methodological focus. Standard single-factor topic representations can entangle those influences. Factorial LDA models several latent dimensions simultaneously so different sources of variation can be separated.

Each document is influenced by K factors, and each word token depends on a K-dimensional latent-variable assignment. Structured word priors and a sparse product of factors guide the model toward an interpretable combination. This lets a token reflect several kinds of contextual influence without requiring them to be collapsed into one topic label.

On research abstracts, the model discovers factors corresponding to research topic, scientific discipline, and methods-versus-applications focus. It improves both held-out perplexity and human interpretability. The contribution links a richer generative structure to more useful corpus organization, showing that separating latent dimensions can help prediction and explanation together.
neurips-2012-factorial-lda-sparse-multi-.tldr: Factorial LDA separates multiple influences on documents through sparse latent-factor products, improving perplexity and interpretability.

paragraphs: Large-scale image recognition requires learning visual features that distinguish many categories across varied high-resolution photographs. This paper trains a deep convolutional network on 1.3 million ImageNet images spanning 1,000 classes. The model brings together substantial capacity and a training implementation able to use that capacity effectively.

The network has about 60 million parameters and 500,000 neurons, with five convolutional layers, pooling in selected locations, and globally connected classification layers. Non-saturating neurons and an efficient GPU implementation accelerate training. A regularization method reduces overfitting in the globally connected portion.

On the LSVRC-2010 test data, top-1 error is 39.7% and top-5 error is 18.9%, substantially better than the preceding results cited by the paper. The contribution demonstrates the combined impact of deep learned features, computational scale, and regularization on a demanding recognition benchmark. The evidence concerns this integrated system rather than isolating one component as the sole cause of the gain.
neurips-2012-imagenet-classification-wit.tldr: A large GPU-trained convolutional network substantially improves ImageNet classification through deep learned features and effective regularization.

paragraphs: Detecting a genuinely new document in a rapid news stream requires a representation that can update without repeatedly processing the whole archive. This paper develops online dictionary learning for that setting. Unlike conventional formulations with squared reconstruction error, it measures reconstruction through an ℓ₁ penalty.

The authors derive an efficient online algorithm using the alternating direction method of multipliers and prove a sublinear regret bound. The learned dictionary adapts as documents arrive, supporting novelty assessment in a changing stream. This turns a batch representation-learning problem into a sequential procedure with a formal performance guarantee.

On news and Twitter data, the method is more than an order of magnitude faster than the previous batch algorithm without significant loss of detection quality. The contribution is both an application to emerging information and a reusable online optimization method. It shows that a representation can remain useful for novelty detection while being updated at streaming scale.
neurips-2012-online-l1-dictionary-learni.tldr: Online ℓ₁ dictionary learning detects novel documents with a sublinear-regret algorithm and much faster updates than the compared batch method.

paragraphs: Methods built for independent binary classification may seem unrelated to comparing highly dependent time series. This paper creates a connection through a new distance between time-series distributions. The distance can be evaluated with binary classification methods, allowing familiar learning tools to support different statistical tasks.

Using that construction, the authors develop algorithms for time-series clustering, homogeneity testing, and the three-sample problem. The classifier acts as a component of distribution comparison rather than simply assigning a conventional class label to each observation. This reduction separates the statistical question from the particular classifier used to help answer it.

Universal consistency is proved under very general assumptions, and synthetic and real-data experiments illustrate the approach. The contribution shows how dependence need not prevent reuse of classification machinery when it is embedded in an appropriate distributional framework. A carefully chosen reduction can transfer algorithms between problem types that initially appear to require entirely different tools.
neurips-2012-reducing-statistical-time-s.tldr: A classification-based distance between time-series distributions yields consistent methods for clustering and distribution-comparison tasks.

paragraphs: Multiple-output regression can improve by sharing structure across its predictive functions, but outputs may also remain dependent after conditioning on the inputs. This paper models both relationships together. It distinguishes similarity among the functions from residual conditional covariance among the output variables.

Neither structure must be supplied in advance; both are learned from data. The model encompasses several earlier structural-regularization methods as special cases. It can also estimate a conditional graphical model among outputs, giving the learned dependencies an interpretation beyond their role in improving prediction.

Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution is a unified view of two sources of statistical sharing that are often treated separately. Learning which predictors should resemble one another and which outputs remain conditionally linked can reveal complementary information, enabling a richer regression model than imposing only one type of covariance structure.
neurips-2012-simultaneously-leveraging-o.tldr: A multiple-output regression model jointly learns relationships among predictive functions and conditional dependencies among outputs.

paragraphs: Principal-component estimation can become fragile when data are heavy-tailed or their marginal distributions differ substantially from Gaussian assumptions. Transelliptical Component Analysis extends a scale-invariant, semiparametric approach to a broad distribution family. It aims to recover a leading latent direction without demanding conventional moment conditions.

The theory gives a near-optimal estimation rate for the leading eigenvector of a latent generalized correlation matrix. The allowed distributions include cases with infinite second moments, no density, and arbitrary continuous marginals. A feature-selection result with an explicit rate further characterizes which coordinates can be identified reliably.

Simulations and large-scale stock data illustrate the method’s usefulness. The contribution combines robustness with high-dimensional statistical guarantees, expanding the range of distributions under which component analysis can be justified. The recovered direction belongs to the latent generalized correlation structure, an important distinction from applying ordinary sample-covariance PCA to heavy-tailed observations.
neurips-2012-transelliptical-component-a.tldr: Transelliptical Component Analysis robustly estimates latent principal directions under broad, potentially very heavy-tailed distributions.

paragraphs: Where people look in an image depends on what they are trying to determine. This paper studies that task dependence through a large eye-tracking extension of VOC 2012 Actions. The dataset includes more than one million fixations over 9,157 images collected during action and context recognition.

The authors learn areas of interest, including their number, location, and spatial extent, and define dynamic consistency measures using those regions. They then infer task-sensitive reward functions from gaze data through inverse optimal control. Those rewards guide planning of subsequent saccades, connecting observed behavior to an explicit decision model.

The analysis shows substantial effects of instructions on gaze, and the resulting method achieves state-of-the-art scanpath modeling. The contribution combines a controlled dataset, evaluation tools, and a predictive mechanism. It makes task goals part of dynamic eye-movement prediction rather than relying on image saliency alone to explain an observer’s sequence of fixations.
neurips-2013-action-from-still-image-dat.tldr: A large task-controlled gaze dataset supports inverse-control learning of rewards that improve prediction of visual scanpaths.

paragraphs: Matrix completion usually evaluates reconstruction of an entire low-rank matrix, but a user may care about one particular missing entry. This paper develops a framework for deciding whether that entry is recoverable and estimating its uncertainty. The focus is local accuracy within an incomplete, noisy matrix.

The authors provide algorithms for entry reconstructability, reconstruction, and denoising, along with prior error bounds for each individual entry. In the noiseless case, reconstruction is exact. For rank-one matrices, the resulting algorithm is fast and supports substantial parallelization.

The rank-one estimator minimizes error in the studied formulation and performs comparably to strong nuclear-norm and OptSpace approaches in the reported comparison. The contribution adds entry-specific reasoning to low-rank recovery: some entries can be well determined even when a global summary is uninformative, and uncertainty can be attached to the actual quantity a downstream user wants.
neurips-2013-error-minimizing-estimates-.tldr: Entry-wise matrix-completion methods determine recoverability, reconstruct individual values, and provide local error bounds, with efficient rank-one algorithms.

paragraphs: Neurons in the macaque superior temporal sulcus combine visual form and motion information relevant to recognizing actors and actions. Population-level decoding had shown useful invariances, but the mechanism at the individual-neuron level remained less clear. This paper tests how much a simple encoding model can explain.

The model takes responses from ventral and dorsal processing streams to short action snippets and combines them through a linear weighted sum. It is fitted to neural recordings to assess whether this modest computation reproduces individual response patterns. The study separates representing an actor regardless of action from representing an action regardless of actor.

The simple model fits the neural data surprisingly well. Even input from one stream can produce either kind of invariance through different linear weights. The contribution suggests that sophisticated population behavior need not require a correspondingly elaborate mechanism at every unit: selective weighting of short visual snippets can already account for important aspects of the observed representations.
neurips-2013-neural-representation-of-ac.tldr: Linear combinations of short action-snippet responses explain substantial STS neural behavior, including actor and action invariance.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval reconstructs a signal from measurements whose magnitudes are known but whose signs or phases are missing. Alternating between phase estimates and signal estimates is a common practical strategy, yet its nonconvex behavior needs justification. This paper proves convergence for a version with Gaussian measurement matrices.

The proposed alternating-minimization algorithm converges geometrically to the solution. Its sample requirement is within logarithmic factors of basic lower bounds, and the analysis extends to nearly optimal scaling for sparse signals. This gives theoretical support to an approach that avoids lifting the problem into a much larger matrix space.

Experiments show sample efficiency and noise robustness comparable to recent convex methods, with much better computational scalability. The contribution combines a rigorous guarantee in a specified random-measurement setting with a practical advantage in large problems. It demonstrates that nonconvex iteration can be both analyzable and efficient when the measurement structure supports the argument.
neurips-2013-phase-retrieval-using-alter.tldr: Alternating minimization achieves geometric phase-retrieval convergence under Gaussian measurements while scaling more efficiently than compared convex lifting methods.

paragraphs: Robust decision-making under an uncertain MDP can optimize the worst possible value or instead limit regret relative to what would have been best for the realized model. This paper develops the latter approach beyond uncertainty only in rewards. It allows both transition dynamics and rewards to vary.

Sampling-based algorithms also accommodate dependencies among uncertainties across states, actions, and decision times. They are designed to improve scalability while retaining quality bounds. A Sample Average Approximation analysis supplies error bounds that can be computed after solving the sampled problem.

Comparisons on two established domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. The contribution makes minimax-regret planning applicable to richer uncertainty descriptions, where independent reward errors would be too restrictive. It also distinguishes the objective from ordinary worst-case planning: the policy is judged by the opportunity it loses relative to the realized model’s best decision, rather than solely by its lowest possible absolute return.
neurips-2013-regret-based-robust-solutio.tldr: Sampling-based minimax-regret algorithms handle correlated uncertainty in both MDP transitions and rewards, with solution-quality bounds.

paragraphs: Binary spike patterns reveal dependencies across a neural population, but low-order maximum-entropy models can miss structure and become computationally difficult at large scale. This paper proposes distributions capable of representing arbitrary patterns while retaining a manageable statistical backbone. Flexibility is combined with a parametric starting model.

A Dirichlet process is centered on a well-behaved base measure, joining histogram-like expressiveness with parametric parsimony. Efficient inference is derived for Bernoulli and cascade-logistic bases. The authors also identify a condition under which the cascade-logistic formulation is equivalent to a second-order Ising model.

Neural-data examples illustrate the resulting models. The contribution permits departures from low-order assumptions without discarding their useful structure entirely. Universality refers to representational capacity over all binary patterns; centering and efficient inference make that broad family usable without requiring a separate freely estimated parameter for every possible pattern from the outset.
neurips-2013-universal-models-for-binary.tldr: Centered Dirichlet-process models flexibly represent neural spike-pattern distributions while retaining efficient inference and useful parametric structure.
